Let

\[
M(m)=\min \int_{-1}^1 f(x)^2\,dx .
\]

The answer is

\[
\boxed{
M(m)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac12+\frac32m^2, & 0\le m\le \frac13,\\[6pt]
\displaystyle 1-\frac16\sqrt{12-24m}, & \frac13\le m\le \frac12.
\end{cases}}
\]

For \(0\le m\le 1/3\), the unconstrained quadratic minimizer is affine:

\[
g(x)=\frac12+\frac{3m}{2}x.
\]

It satisfies \(0\le g\le 1\) exactly when \(m\le 1/3\), and has the required moments. For any admissible \(f\),

\[
\int_{-1}^1 f^2
=
\int_{-1}^1 g^2+\int_{-1}^1 (f-g)^2
\ge \int_{-1}^1 g^2,
\]

because \(g\) is affine and \(f-g\) has zero zeroth and first moments. Hence

\[
M(m)=\int_{-1}^1\left(\frac12+\frac{3m}{2}x\right)^2dx
=\frac12+\frac32m^2.
\]

For \(1/3\le m\le 1/2\), set

\[
L=\sqrt{12-24m}\in[0,2],
\]

and define

\[
g(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & -1\le x\le -L/2,\\
\displaystyle \frac{x+L/2}{L}, & -L/2\le x\le L/2,\\
1, & L/2\le x\le 1.
\end{cases}
\]

Then

\[
\int_{-1}^1 g(x)\,dx=\frac L2+\left(1-\frac L2\right)=1,
\]

and

\[
\int_{-1}^1 xg(x)\,dx
=
\frac{L^2}{12}+\frac12\left(1-\frac{L^2}{4}\right)
=
\frac12-\frac{L^2}{24}
=m.
\]

Also

\[
\int_{-1}^1 g(x)^2\,dx
=
\frac L3+\left(1-\frac L2\right)
=
1-\frac L6.
\]

It remains to prove optimality. Define the affine function

\[
\lambda(x)=\frac{2}{L}\left(x+\frac L2\right).
\]

For every \(u\in[0,1]\),

\[
u^2-g(x)^2\ge \lambda(x)(u-g(x)).
\]

Indeed, on the ramp this is equality to first order since \(\lambda=2g\); on the left, \(g=0\) and \(\lambda\le0\), so \(u^2\ge \lambda u\); on the right, \(g=1\) and \(\lambda\ge2\), so \(u^2-1\ge \lambda(u-1)\).

Applying this with \(u=f(x)\) and integrating,

\[
\int f^2-\int g^2
\ge
\int \lambda(x)(f(x)-g(x))\,dx=0,
\]

because \(\lambda\) is affine and \(f,g\) have the same zeroth and first moments. Thus \(g\) is optimal.

At \(m=1/3\), both formulas give \(2/3\); at \(m=1/2\), the minimizer is \(g=\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}\), giving value \(1\).
